\chapter{Sit, and How You Feel}
\label{ch:mr-wellbeing-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can run a short visit in Marathi -- seat my guest, say how I feel on the dative frame, say that I am sleepy, and accept an offer with chalel.}

Complete MR-R23-wellbeing-verbs and produce the whole small scene from memory: basa, mala baram vatam, chalel -- then name which of the four verbs Marathi built for itself rather than inheriting.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[basṇe]{\mr{बसणे} (basṇe) — to sit}

\label{lesson:MR-C23-basne}



\begin{quote}
The last run of words was about things. This one is about how a person is doing — and it opens with what a Marathi household says to a visitor before anything else.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{बसणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बसणे}} — \emph{basṇe} — \textbf{to sit}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{बसा}.} — \emph{basā.} — \textbf{Please sit.}
\end{quote}

One word, and it is hospitality: said at the door, it means \emph{you are welcome, stay a while}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{बसतो} / \mr{बसते}.} — \emph{mī basto / baste.} — \textbf{I sit.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{ब}} the quiet \emph{ba}, \textbf{\mr{स}} the \emph{sa} of \emph{namaskār}, and \textbf{\mr{णे}} as ever. \textbf{\mr{ब}-\mr{स}-\mr{णे}}. Nothing here is new to your hand.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{बसणे}} comes through Prakrit \textbf{vaisai} from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{उपविशति}} \emph{upaviśati}, \textquotedblleft{}sits down\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{\mr{उप}} \emph{upa-}, \textquotedblleft{}down, near,\textquotedblright{} on \textbf{\mr{विश्}} \emph{viś-}, \textquotedblleft{}to enter, to settle in.\textquotedblright{}

That settling root is Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*wey\'{k}-}}, which named the dwelling and then the group of people in it. Latin took it as \emph{vīcus}, a village or a quarter of a town, and English carries it, worn thin, at the end of place names: \textbf{Norwich}, \textbf{Warwick}, \textbf{Ipswich}. To sit down and to settle a village turn out to be the same idea at two sizes.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{basṇe} — to sit
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{basā.} — please sit, the way a host says it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mī basto} or \textbf{mī baste}, whichever declares you
  \item \emph{Name:} what Latin \emph{vīcus} meant — \textbf{a village}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Invite someone to sit. (\textbf{Basā.}) What did the root under \textbf{\mr{बसणे}} mean before it meant sitting? (\textbf{To settle, to enter a dwelling}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AC\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{बसणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%B6\%E0\%A5\%8D}{Wiktionary: \mr{विश्}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vāṭṇe]{\mr{वाटणे} (vāṭṇe) — to feel, to seem}

\label{lesson:MR-C23-vatne}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs you own put you in the dative rather than the nominative: \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{मराठी} \mr{आवडते}} and \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे}}. A third one joins them now, and it is the one you answer \emph{how are you} with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{वाटणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{वाटणे}} — \emph{vāṭṇe} — \textbf{to feel, to seem}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{बरं} \mr{वाटतं}.} — \emph{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ.} — \textbf{I feel fine.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third verb that puts you in the dative}]
Word for word, \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{बरं} \mr{वाटतं}} is \emph{to-me fine seems}. You are not the one doing the feeling; the feeling arrives at you, and \textbf{\mr{मला}} \emph{malā} is where it lands. Three sentences now stand on that one frame:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे}} — to me it is known
  \item \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{मराठी} \mr{आवडते}} — to me Marathi is pleasing
  \item \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{बरं} \mr{वाटतं}} — to me fine seems
\end{itemize}

Marathi keeps saying that what happens inside a person happens \emph{to} them. Once that click lands, a whole family of verbs opens at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{व}}, \textbf{\mr{ा}}, \textbf{\mr{ट}} — the retroflex \emph{ṭa}, tongue curled back — then \textbf{\mr{णे}}. \textbf{\mr{वा}-\mr{ट}-\mr{णे}}. In \textbf{\mr{वाटतं}} the final \textbf{\mr{तं}} carries the neuter ending that \textbf{\mr{बरं}} also wears.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{vāṭṇe} — to feel, to seem
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ.} — I feel fine
  \item \emph{Run through:} the three dative sentences in order — \textbf{malā māhīt āhe}, \textbf{malā marāṭhī āvaḍte}, \textbf{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} what \textbf{malā} does in all three — it is where the feeling arrives
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\mr{बरं}} on its own, the agreeing word you have had since the first courtesy run, and hear it doing new work inside this sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say that you feel fine. (\textbf{Malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ.}) Translated word for word, what does that sentence say? (\textbf{To me fine seems}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%9F\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{वाटणे}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jhopṇe]{\mr{झोपणे} (jhopṇe) — to sleep}

\label{lesson:MR-C23-jhopne}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{डोळा}} turned out not to be the old inherited eye-word at all — Marathi had swapped it for something else entirely. That happened more than once, and here is the second case.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{झोपणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{झोपणे}} — \emph{jhopṇe} — \textbf{to sleep}
\end{quote}

The noun sits inside it: \textbf{\mr{झोप}} \emph{jhop}, \textquotedblleft{}sleep.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{झोप} \mr{येते}.} — \emph{malā jhop yete.} — \textbf{I am sleepy.}
\end{quote}

Word for word: \emph{to me sleep comes}. The dative frame you met a moment ago is already back at work, and the form carrying it is \textbf{\mr{येते}} — the very leave- taking word you learned in your first courtesy run, doing a different job here.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{झ}} is the breathy \emph{jha} you have from \emph{mājhaṁ}; \textbf{\mr{ो}} the familiar \emph{o} mark; \textbf{\mr{प}} and \textbf{\mr{णे}} are old friends. \textbf{\mr{झो}-\mr{प}-\mr{णे}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
The inherited Indo-Aryan verb for sleeping is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{स्वपिति}} \emph{svapiti}, and Hindi still uses its descendant: \textbf{\mr{सोना}} \emph{sonā}. Behind it stands Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*swep-}}, which Latin took as \emph{sopor}, \textquotedblleft{}deep sleep\textquotedblright{} — so English \textbf{soporific} is a cousin of Hindi's word for going to bed.

Marathi's \textbf{\mr{झोपणे}} is not that word. It rests on native \textbf{\mr{झोप}}, whose pre-Marathi ancestry is not securely established, and this lesson does not invent one for it. What can be said is the pattern: with the eye, and again with sleep, Marathi let the inherited word go and built on something of its own.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jhopṇe} — to sleep
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{malā jhop yete.} — I am sleepy, \textquotedblleft{}to me sleep comes\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{basā}, then \textbf{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ}, then \textbf{malā jhop yete}
  \item \emph{Name:} the English word that is cousin to Hindi's sleep-word — \textbf{soporific}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say that you are sleepy. (\textbf{Malā jhop yete.}) Is \textbf{\mr{झोपणे}} the same word as Hindi's \textbf{\mr{सोना}}? (\textbf{No} — Marathi built its own, as it did with the eye.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9D\%E0\%A5\%8B\%E0\%A4\%AA}{Wiktionary: \mr{झोप}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%AA\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: svapiti}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chālṇe]{\mr{चालणे} (chālṇe) — to walk, and the yes that comes out of it}

\label{lesson:MR-C23-chalne}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{विचार}} rested on a root meaning \emph{to turn, to move about}. Its close relative walks in here on its own two feet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{चालणे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चालणे}} — \emph{chālṇe} — \textbf{to walk, to go along}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{चालतो} / \mr{चालते}.} — \emph{mī chālto / chālte.} — \textbf{I walk.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\mr{च}} before \textbf{\mr{ा}} lands closer to English \emph{ts} than to \emph{ch} in most Marathi mouths, so \textbf{\mr{चा}} is nearer \emph{tsā} — the same thing that happens in \emph{chār}. Then \textbf{\mr{ल}} and \textbf{\mr{णे}}. \textbf{\mr{चा}-\mr{ल}-\mr{णे}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the yes that means it will walk}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{चालेल}.} — \emph{chālel.} — \textbf{That will do. / Fine by me.}
\end{quote}

Formally this is the verb in the future: \emph{it will walk}. In use it is one of the commonest small yeses in the language — offered a time, a plan, a cup of tea, you answer \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} and the matter is settled. Beside \textbf{\mr{बरं}}, which agrees, \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} accepts.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\mr{चालणे}} continues Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{चलति}} \emph{calati}, \textquotedblleft{}moves, stirs,\textquotedblright{} on the root \textbf{\mr{चल्}} \emph{cal-}, which is widely taken to be a variant of \textbf{\mr{चर्}} \emph{car-}, \textquotedblleft{}to move about\textquotedblright{} — the root you already met sitting inside \textbf{\mr{विचार}}. Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{चंचल}} \emph{cañcala}, \textquotedblleft{}restless,\textquotedblright{} is built on the same piece. So thinking and walking, in this language, are two speeds of one old verb for moving.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chālṇe} — to walk
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mī chālto} or \textbf{mī chālte}, whichever declares you
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{chālel.} — that will do
  \item \emph{Run through:} someone asks how you are; answer \textbf{malā baraṁ vāṭtaṁ}, then accept their offer with \textbf{chālel}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Accept an offer in one word. (\textbf{Chālel.}) What is \textbf{\mr{चालेल}} literally? (\textbf{It will walk}.) Which word you already knew stands on the same moving root? (\textbf{\mr{विचार}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%A3\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{चालणे}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%9A\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: \mr{चलति}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[basā / vāṭtaṁ / jhop / chālel]{One visit, four verbs}

\label{lesson:MR-R23-wellbeing-verbs}



\begin{quote}
Say the four infinitives in order: \textbf{\mr{बसणे}, \mr{वाटणे}, \mr{झोपणे}, \mr{चालणे}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Run it once as a small scene, then repair only what went missing.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four is a word Marathi built for itself instead of keeping the inherited one? (\textbf{\mr{झोपणे}}.) Which one goes back to a root for settling a dwelling? (\textbf{\mr{बसणे}}.) When you answer that you are well, which word carries the \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\mr{बरं}}.) And which body word have you met for the place feeling is said to sit? (\textbf{\mr{हृदय}}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
